title: Optical Control of Living Cells Electrical Activity by Conjugated Polymers
protocol: Prepare a P3HT:PCBM solution at a P3HT concentration of 20 g/L in chlorobenzene.
Mix the P3HT:PCBM solution with a magnetic stirrer for at least 4 hours at 60°C.
Clean ITO-coated glass slides with deionized water, acetone, and isopropanol successively using a sonicator for 10 minutes each step.
Dry the cleaned coverslips with a nitrogen gun.
Place the samples in a plasma cleaner at 100 W power for 10 minutes.
Deposit a thin film of the active layer on the cleaned ITO-coated substrates via spin-coating.
Cut a microscope glass slide to match the dimensions of the ITO-coated substrate using a diamond tip.
Let the P3HT:PCBM solution cool to ambient temperature after removing it from the hotplate.
Set up a two-step spin-coater program: 30 seconds at 800 rpm followed by 30 seconds at 1,600 rpm.
Place the cleaned substrate on the chuck of the spin-coater and start the vacuum to secure it.
Put a drop of acetone on the substrate to remove excess solvent.
Add 150 µl of P3HT:PCBM solution onto the substrate.
Start the spin-coater using the two-step program described earlier.
Remove the sample from the spin-coater after it has finished.
Carefully detach the coated substrate from the glass slide.
Clean the back of the substrate with a cleanroom swab dipped in acetone.
Prepare the complete growth medium (CGM) for HEK-293 cells by supplementing DMEM with 10% FBS, 100 U/ml penicillin, and 100 µg/ml streptomycin.
Sterilize the complete growth medium with a 0.2 μm filtration system.
Store the sterilized CGM at 4 °C.
Prepare the extracellular solution in ultrapure water by mixing: 135 mM NaCl, 5.4 mM KCl, 5 mM HEPES, 10 mM Glucose, 1.8 mM CaCl2, and 1 mM MgCl2.
Adjust the pH of the extracellular solution to 7.4 with NaOH.
Sterilize the extracellular solution with a 0.2 μm filtration system.
Store the sterilized extracellular solution at 4 °C.
Prepare the intracellular solution in ultrapure water by mixing: 12 mM KCl, 125 mM K-Gluconate, 1 mM MgCl2, 0.1 mM CaCl2, 10 mM EGTA, and 10 mM HEPES.
Add ATP-Na2 last to the intracellular solution.
Adjust the pH of the intracellular solution to 7.4 with NaOH.
Sterilize the intracellular solution with a 0.2 μm filtration system.
Aliquot the sterilized intracellular solution in 1 ml tubes and store at -20 °C.
Place the photoactive substrate in a glass beaker covered with aluminum or a closed Petri dish.
Put the beaker or Petri dish in an oven at 120 °C for 2 hours for sterilization.
Remove the substrate from the oven and place it in a sterile hood to cool down.
Coat the photoactive substrate with an adhesion layer to reduce surface hydrophobicity and promote cell adhesion.
Mix PDMS and catalyst in a 10:1 proportion with a glass rod to obtain a viscous slurry.
Pour the slurry into a 6 multiwell plate, dispensing enough to cover half of each well.
Wait for PDMS polymerization at room temperature.
Cut the cured PDMS in the middle to form square shapes matching the dimension of the polymer sample.
Sterilize the PDMS wells by immersing them in a 70% ethanol-water mixture for at least 30 minutes.
Scratch the photoactive layer along the entire border of each well with pointed tweezers.
Cover the entire surface of each sample with a fibronectin solution (2 mg/L in PBS).
Incubate the samples at 37 °C for at least 1 hr.
Remove the fibronectin solution with a glass pipette.
Wash once with 2 ml of PBS.
Plate HEK-293 cells on the fibronectin-treated samples at a density of 15,000 cells/cm² in complete growth medium.
Incubate the cells at 37 °C and 5% CO₂ for 24-48 hr.
Put the extracellular solution in a water bath at 37 °C to thermalize.
Thaw the intracellular solution.
Place the thawed intracellular solution in a 1 ml syringe with a 34 gauge needle.
Keep the syringe in contact with ice to avoid degradation of ATP.
Take a cell-coated substrate from the incubator, carefully removing the PDMS well if present.
Remove the growth medium with a glass pipette.
Rinse the sample with extracellular solution.
Put the device into the sample-holder of the electrophysiology station with extracellular solution and the reference electrode.
Prepare fresh glass micropipettes for patch-clamp with a puller (ideal resistance is in the range 2-4 MΩ).
Fill half of the pipette with intracellular solution.
Mount the filled pipette on the micromanipulator.
Look for a healthy cell to patch on the device.
Use IR illumination for imaging, placing a long-wavelength pass filter (for example, a cut wavelength λ = 750 nm) in front of the microscope illuminator.
Patch the selected cell.
Apply the desired protocol for optical stimulation by delivering light to the sample via the fluorescence excitation path of the microscope.
Position the patch pipette in close proximity to the cell membrane with a micrometric manipulator.
During positioning, apply overpressure to the pipette to avoid dirt sticking on the tip.
Ensure the pipette is few microns above the cell.
Start lowering the pipette towards the cell membrane while controlling the pipette resistance on the patch control software.
Increase the pipette resistance to about 1 GΩ by applying gentle suction.
Remove overpressure from the pipette and apply gentle suction to form a gigaseal between the pipette and the cell membrane.
Apply a negative potential of -40 mV to the pipette to stabilize the seal for HEK293 cells.
Compensate capacitive transients due to pipette capacitance with commands on the patch amplifier or control software.
Apply a brief, intense suction pulse to break the membrane and allow electrical access to the cell cytoplasm.
Set the patch amplifier to current clamp mode (I = 0) to track the cell membrane potential.
Wait for several minutes to ensure stability of the cell's membrane potential.
Apply the desired illumination protocol to the cell and record its effect on the membrane potential.
Select an excitation wavelength between 450-600 nm for the P3HT:PCBM blend.
Set photoexcitation densities within the range of 10-100 mW/mm².
Use short pulses of light (below 10-20 msec) to induce transient depolarization in cells.
Apply prolonged illumination (hundreds of milliseconds or longer pulses) to achieve sustained hyperpolarization.
